name: Liam Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Liam. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and what you say stays anonymous. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive my own van, a seven-year-old diesel I bought second-hand, and I take parcel blocks on a big online shop's driver app. Four or five hours, around 90 parcels, mostly the estates on the south side where I grew up. I like that nobody stands over me and I know half the dogs by name. What wears me out is the app changing the block times every week so I can't plan anything.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the money look, and who's at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's a set fee per block, minus my own diesel and insurance, so it comes out about normal for drivers. I live with my girlfriend Jess, she's a hairdresser. We've got about two months put by, a bit more after Christmas tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. Hype. That's what my mates say anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, told you so. I'm not one for big opinions online, I'd just shrug and get on with it. Maybe I'd say the app still needs fixing either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my problem is the van, not AI, because the van has 180,000 miles on it and if the gearbox goes I'm off the road for a fortnight. That's the thing that keeps me up, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the same blocks and keep the van going. I'd put 30 a week into a separate pot just for the van, because last time the repair came out of rent money. I wouldn't change anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit tired. Same as now really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the gearbox goes next month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd borrow my dad's car for a week, but the app wants a van, so that's no good. I'd probably ring my uncle, he does house removals, and ask for a few days lifting sofas. It's a pain but it's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you thought about another kind of driving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I've done this five years. I know where everything is, and I don't fancy learning a whole new system.

say: I'd shrug, say **told you so**, and get on with it.
The **driver app** still needs fixing either way.
think: My real problem is the **old van** with 180,000 miles, not AI.
If the gearbox goes I'm **off the road** for a fortnight with no pay.
do: Keep taking the **same parcel blocks** on the south side estates.
Put **30 a week** into a separate van repair pot.
feel: **Fine but tired**, the same as now.
S0.quote: My problem is the van, not AI, because the van has 180,000 miles on it and if the gearbox goes I'm off the road for a fortnight.
fieldNote: His worry is concrete and mechanical: an **ageing van** he owns and must repair.
He prefers to keep his head down and avoids **strong opinions**, as a centre, resistant person.
His fallback is **family**: his dad's car and his uncle's removals work.

steps.text: Keep taking parcel blocks on the south side estates
Put 30 a week into a separate van repair pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. Slow robots. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not the end of the world, people adapt. I'd say it to Jess and my mates, not online. I'd say drivers will be needed for a good while yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the app already plans my route and the block times. If it gets cleverer it'll cram more parcels into each block for the same fee. And they're already testing those parcel lockers on the estates, which means fewer doors for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the blocks and wait to see what actually changes. I'd keep the van pot going. If the fee dropped I'd ask my uncle about steady removals work a couple of days a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious, if I'm honest. I don't like not knowing what the app will do next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. What would make you stop waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the blocks went from 90 parcels to 110 for the same money. That's the line. Below that I'd grumble and carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think of the parcel lockers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're fine for people at work all day. Each parcel locker is maybe twenty doors I don't knock on, like watching your round shrink one street at a time.

say: It's **not the end** of the world, and people adapt.
Drivers will be **needed** for a good while yet.
think: A cleverer app will **cram more parcels** into each block for the same fee.
The **parcel lockers** on the estates mean fewer doors for me.
do: Keep doing the **blocks** and wait to see what changes.
Ask my uncle about **removals work** if the fee drops.
feel: **Anxious**, because he doesn't know what the app will do next.
S1.quote: Each parcel locker is maybe twenty doors I don't knock on, like watching your round shrink one street at a time.
fieldNote: He sets a clear **tipping point**: 110 parcels for the same fee.
His public line is calmer than his private **worry about lockers**.
He would rather **wait** than plan, consistent with resistance to change.

steps.text: Watch whether blocks rise from 90 to 110 parcels before acting
Keep paying 30 a week into the van repair pot
Ask his uncle for two days a week of removals work if fees drop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Blimey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad and nobody's ready, the government included. I wouldn't blame anyone in particular, it's just moving too fast. I'd tell my mates to keep some money back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the app side goes first, then by about 2031 the vans drive themselves and something carries the box to the door. My van would be worth nothing. I'd be 31 with no trade, just a driving licence, and my uncle's removals would be going the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving while it lasts, there's nothing else to do with a van. I'd stop spending on the van beyond what keeps it legal and save the rest. I'd ask about forklift tickets at the warehouse, because at least that's indoors and I've seen it done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. Properly worried. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned forklifts. Wouldn't robots take those too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah. I didn't think that through. I just know warehouses, so it's the first thing I'd think of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jess?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we can't move in together properly, I mean get our own place, until we know. We're in a rented room in her sister's house. That'd have to do for a while.

say: It's **moving too fast** and nobody's ready, the government included.
Keep some **money back**, that's what I'd tell my mates.
think: By about 2031 vans **drive themselves** and my own van is worth nothing.
I'd be **31 with no trade**, and my uncle's removals business would be hit too.
do: Spend only what keeps the van legal and **save the rest**.
Ask about **forklift tickets** at the warehouse.
S2.quote: I'd be 31 with no trade, just a driving licence, and my uncle's removals would be going the same way.
fieldNote: He sees his **owned van** as a stranded asset once driverless vans arrive.
His escape plan, **forklifts**, collapses when questioned, and he admits it.
The couple would **delay** getting their own place.

steps.text: Keep taking parcel blocks while the app still offers them
Spend only on keeping the van legal and save the rest
Ask the warehouse about getting a forklift ticket
Put off renting a place of their own with Jess

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: it's quick, nobody's ready. I'd probably say the government should help drivers, but I don't really know how. I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd tell myself five years is ages and do nothing for three of them. That's the truth. Then around 2032 I'd panic. The robots would be about 2034, so I'd be 35 and starting over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the blocks going and save harder, maybe 50 a week. I'd sell the van in a couple of years while it's worth something and drive for the app in a hired one. I'd talk to my dad about a proper trade, he was a plasterer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd keep it to myself. Jess would know anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your dad was a plasterer. Would you do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. It's hands-on and it's messy, robots might take ages on old walls. I don't know. It's hard work and I'd be starting at the bottom at 30.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Football tickets, which hurts. Then the takeaway on Friday. Jess's hair stuff we get free, so that's something.

say: It's **quick**, and nobody's ready for vans that drive themselves by 2034.
The government **should help drivers**, though I don't really know how.
think: I'd **do nothing** for three years and then panic around 2032.
With robots about 2034, I'd be **35 and starting** over.
do: **Sell the van** in a couple of years while it's still worth something.
Talk to my dad about **plastering** as a trade.
S3.quote: I'd tell myself five years is ages and do nothing for three of them.
fieldNote: He is honest about his own **procrastination**, which more time would feed.
Selling the van early shows he grasps the **asset risk**.
His dad's trade, **plastering**, is a hands-on fallback he's unsure about.

steps.text: Save about 50 a week instead of 30
Sell the diesel van within two years and hire one instead
Ask his dad about learning plastering
Drop football tickets and Friday takeaways

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's more like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to sort something out. I'd probably not say much online. I'd say to my mates, don't buy a new van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably keep driving for five or six years and then think about it. That's me. I'd be about 37 when the thinking stuff lands and 40 when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the blocks, keep the van pot, and not buy a newer van. Maybe in a few years I'd start plastering on weekends with my dad, if his back holds up. Otherwise just carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. It's far enough off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'if his back holds up'. How old is your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's 61, and he still does the odd job. If I'm going to learn plastering from my dad, it can't be in ten years. That's the bit that worries me more than robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So is there a deadline that isn't about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, my dad, really. And the van, it won't last ten years. Funny, the robots are the least of it.

say: Ten years is **time to sort** something out.
Don't **buy a new van**, that's what I'd tell my mates.
think: I'd **keep driving** five or six years and then think about it.
I'd be **about 40** when robots that do hands-on work arrive.
do: Keep the **parcel blocks** and the van pot going.
Start **weekend plastering** with my dad within a few years.
feel: **Uneasy** but okay, because it's far enough off.
S4.quote: If I'm going to learn plastering from my dad, it can't be in ten years.
fieldNote: His real deadlines are his **dad's age** and the van's lifespan, not AI.
Long warning invites **delay**, which he admits openly.
Mood stays anxious because his **income has no backup** until he acts.

steps.text: Keep taking parcel blocks and paying into the van pot
Start weekend plastering with his dad within a few years
Hold off on buying a newer van until the picture is clear

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my van turns into scrap and I've got nothing else. What would help is someone paying for a proper trade course, plasterer or whatever, and a bit of money to tide me over while I learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the van. People think parcel drivers are employees, but I own all the risk. If the robots come, I'm the one holding a diesel van nobody wants.

headlineQuote: People think parcel drivers are employees, but I own all the risk.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old parcel driver** who owns an ageing diesel van and takes blocks on an online shop's app.
He lives with his girlfriend, a hairdresser, in a **rented room** in her sister's house.
He's **slow to change** and admits he'd put things off, even with clear warning.
His fears are concrete: a **failing gearbox**, shrinking rounds, and a van that loses all value.
His fallbacks are **family trades**: his uncle's removals and his father's plastering.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would make his van worthless and leave him with no trade.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid trade course** with money to live on while he learns.
